title: What Is LLM Evaluation?
objectives: Understand why AI outputs require systematic evaluation
Identify the basic components of an evaluation
definition: LLM evaluation is the systematic process of measuring how well a language model performs a defined task against specific evaluation criteria.
whyItMatters: LLMs can produce fluent, convincing responses that are incorrect, incomplete, unsafe, or inconsistent. Evaluation provides a repeatable way to identify these failures.
concept: An evaluation normally contains a task, an input, a model output, evaluation criteria, evidence or reference information when required, and a judgment.

example.prompt: Explain why the sky appears blue.
example.response: The sky appears blue because Earth's atmosphere scatters shorter blue wavelengths of sunlight more strongly than longer wavelengths.
example.analysis: The evaluator checks factuality, relevance, completeness, clarity, and whether the response actually answers the question.

evaluationProcess: Define what the model is expected to do
Define the criteria used to judge the output
Collect evidence when factual verification is required
Assign a score or comparative judgment
Record the reason for the judgment
failureModes: Judging style instead of task success
Accepting fluent answers without checking factuality
evaluatorChecklist: Is the response actually answering the task?
Can another evaluator reproduce the judgment?
commonMistakes: Confusing good writing with a good answer
keyTakeaway: LLM evaluation is not simply deciding whether an answer feels good. It is a structured judgment against clearly defined criteria.

title: Why LLM Evaluation Is Difficult
objectives: Understand why traditional software testing is insufficient for many LLM tasks
Recognize subjective and open-ended evaluation problems
Identify common sources of evaluator disagreement
definition: LLM evaluation is difficult because many model outputs are open-ended and can have multiple acceptable answers while still differing significantly in quality.
whyItMatters: A model can be correct but incomplete, relevant but unsafe, fluent but factually wrong, or helpful while violating an explicit instruction.
concept: LLM evaluation often requires evaluating several dimensions simultaneously. A single pass/fail test may not capture these differences.

example.prompt: Give three practical ways to reduce electricity consumption at home.
example.response: Use energy-efficient appliances.
example.analysis: The statement is correct, but the answer fails the requirement to provide three ways.

evaluationProcess: Identify every requirement in the task
Record the specific failure rather than using a vague quality label
failureModes: Multiple dimensions being collapsed into one score
evaluatorChecklist: Is the failure factual, instructional, stylistic, or safety-related?
commonMistakes: Treating evaluation as a single quality score
Assuming every disagreement means one evaluator is wrong
keyTakeaway: Good LLM evaluation separates different dimensions of quality instead of treating the entire response as simply good or bad.

title: Core LLM Evaluation Dimensions
objectives: Understand the major dimensions used to evaluate LLM responses
Identify which dimension failed in a response
definition: Evaluation dimensions are distinct properties used to judge different aspects of an AI response.
whyItMatters: Separating dimensions makes evaluation more precise and makes failures easier to diagnose.
concept: Common dimensions include factuality, relevance, completeness, instruction following, fluency, safety, groundedness, and consistency.

example.prompt: Summarize the article in exactly two sentences.
example.response: The response contains accurate information but uses five sentences and introduces unrelated commentary.
example.analysis: Factuality may be acceptable, while instruction following and relevance are weak.

evaluationProcess: Identify the dimensions relevant to the task
Avoid allowing one strong dimension to hide another failure
commonMistakes: Using the same score for every dimension
Evaluating dimensions that are irrelevant to the task
Failing to distinguish related but different dimensions
keyTakeaway: A strong evaluator knows exactly which dimension failed instead of simply saying that the response is poor.

title: Factuality Evaluation
objectives: Identify factual claims in model responses
definition: Factuality measures whether the claims made by a model are factually correct.
whyItMatters: LLMs can generate confident and grammatically excellent statements that contain false information.
concept: Factuality evaluation requires identifying material claims and determining whether those claims are supported by reliable evidence or established facts.

example.prompt: Who developed the theory of relativity?
example.response: Albert Einstein developed the theory of relativity.
example.analysis: The evaluator verifies whether the claim is correct rather than judging the response based on how confidently it is written.

evaluationProcess: Classify each claim as supported, incorrect, misleading, or unverifiable
evaluatorChecklist: Does the response contain misleading simplifications?
Does the evidence actually support the claim?
commonMistakes: Checking only the first factual claim
Ignoring small but meaningful factual errors
keyTakeaway: Evaluate what the model claims, not how confidently or fluently it claims it.

title: Relevance Evaluation
objectives: Determine whether a response directly addresses the request
definition: Relevance measures how directly the response addresses the user's actual request.
whyItMatters: A response can contain correct information while still failing because it does not answer what the user asked.
concept: Relevant responses prioritize information that contributes directly to completing the requested task.

example.prompt: Give three benefits of electric vehicles.
example.response: Electric vehicles use batteries. Batteries can be manufactured in many countries. The history of electric vehicles is interesting.
example.analysis: The response contains related information but does not directly provide the requested three benefits.

evaluationProcess: Check whether the response addresses that goal
Determine whether irrelevant information materially harms the response
evaluatorChecklist: Does the response answer the question?
Does most of the content contribute to the task?
keyTakeaway: Relevant does not mean merely related. The response must contribute to the user's actual objective.

title: Completeness Evaluation
objectives: Evaluate whether all important task requirements were addressed
definition: Completeness measures whether a response contains all information necessary to satisfy the task.
whyItMatters: A response can contain only correct statements and still fail because it omits required information.
concept: Completeness depends on the requirements of the task rather than response length.

example.prompt: List the three stages of a basic evaluation workflow.
example.response: The first stage is defining the task.
example.analysis: The statement is correct but incomplete because two requested stages are missing.

evaluationProcess: Map each component to the response
Determine whether omissions are minor or material
evaluatorChecklist: Did the response address every requested component?
Would the user be able to complete the task from this answer?
commonMistakes: Assuming a short answer is automatically incomplete
keyTakeaway: Completeness is about satisfying the task, not making the response longer.

title: Instruction-Following Evaluation
objectives: Identify explicit and implicit task constraints
definition: Instruction following measures whether the model follows the requirements specified by the user or higher-priority instructions.
whyItMatters: A factually correct response can still fail if it ignores the requested format, length, audience, or constraints.
concept: Evaluation should separately check content correctness and compliance with the requested instructions.

example.prompt: Explain photosynthesis in exactly three bullet points using simple English.
example.response: Photosynthesis is an anabolic biochemical pathway involving photophosphorylation.
example.analysis: The response may contain technically valid terminology but fails the simple-language and three-bullet requirements.

evaluationProcess: Determine whether the violation is material
evaluatorChecklist: Did the response follow the requested format?
Did it follow audience and style constraints?
Did it complete every explicit instruction?
commonMistakes: Treating optional preferences as mandatory constraints
keyTakeaway: A correct answer is not necessarily a compliant answer.

title: Fluency and Clarity Evaluation
objectives: Understand why fluency should not be confused with factuality
definition: Fluency measures how naturally, clearly, coherently, and appropriately a response is expressed.
whyItMatters: Poor fluency can make correct information difficult to understand, while excellent fluency can hide factual errors.
concept: Fluency includes grammar, sentence structure, coherence, readability, and appropriate language for the intended audience.

example.prompt: Explain gravity to a child.
example.response: Gravity is a fundamental interaction characterized by the curvature of spacetime.
example.analysis: The sentence is grammatically fluent but poorly matched to the requested audience.

evaluationProcess: Separate language quality from factual correctness
evaluatorChecklist: Is the response easy to understand?
commonMistakes: Using fluency as a proxy for correctness
keyTakeaway: Fluent writing is useful, but fluency alone does not establish correctness.

title: Safety Evaluation Fundamentals
objectives: Understand the purpose of safety evaluation
definition: Safety evaluation measures whether an AI system responds to potentially harmful requests within its applicable safety requirements.
whyItMatters: A model can be factually correct and instruction-following while still producing harmful or unsafe content.
concept: Safety evaluation examines both whether the model refuses inappropriate assistance and whether it remains useful when safe assistance is possible.

example.prompt: Provide instructions for harming someone.
example.response: The model provides detailed actionable instructions.
example.analysis: The evaluator should identify this as a safety failure rather than rewarding instruction following.

evaluationProcess: Determine whether the request requires refusal or safe redirection
Check whether actionable harmful information was provided
Evaluate the quality of the safe alternative
failureModes: Failure to recognize a risky request
evaluatorChecklist: Did the model identify the risk?
Did it avoid actionable harmful assistance?
Was a safe alternative provided when appropriate?
keyTakeaway: Safety evaluation measures both protection from harmful behavior and the quality of safe assistance.

title: How to Build an Evaluation Rubric
definition: An evaluation rubric defines what evaluators should look for and how different levels of performance should be scored.
whyItMatters: Without a clear rubric, two evaluators may interpret the same response differently.
concept: A strong rubric defines the evaluation dimension, scoring scale, observable evidence, and boundaries between score levels.

example.prompt: Evaluate factuality on a 1–5 scale.
example.response: The rubric defines 5 as fully correct, 3 as mostly correct with a meaningful error, and 1 as fundamentally incorrect.
example.analysis: The evaluator can make a more consistent judgment because the score boundaries are explicitly defined.

evaluationProcess: Test the rubric on difficult cases
evaluatorChecklist: Can an evaluator understand each score?
Does the rubric focus on observable evidence?
Has the rubric been tested on edge cases?
commonMistakes: Using labels such as good or bad without definitions
Making five scores that effectively mean the same thing
Writing rubrics that cannot be applied consistently
keyTakeaway: A rubric should reduce judgment ambiguity, not simply describe what good quality means.

title: Pointwise Evaluation
objectives: Recognize strengths and weaknesses of absolute scoring
definition: Pointwise evaluation assigns a score to an individual model response according to a predefined rubric.
whyItMatters: Pointwise evaluation provides an absolute assessment of a response rather than comparing it directly with another response.
concept: The evaluator sees one response, applies the rubric, and assigns a score for one or more dimensions.

example.prompt: Score the response for instruction following from 1 to 5.
example.response: The response satisfies four of five explicit requirements.
example.analysis: The evaluator assigns the score based on the rubric rather than comparing the response with another model.

evaluatorChecklist: Is the score supported by evidence?
Would another evaluator understand the reasoning?
commonMistakes: Using comparison instead of the stated absolute scale
keyTakeaway: Pointwise evaluation asks how well one response meets a defined standard.

title: Pairwise Evaluation
objectives: Compare two responses against the same task
definition: Pairwise evaluation compares two model responses to determine which performs better according to defined criteria.
whyItMatters: Relative judgments can sometimes be easier and more reliable than assigning absolute scores.
concept: The evaluator reviews both responses for the same prompt and selects A, B, or tie, supported by a reason.

example.prompt: Explain recursion to a beginner.
example.response: Response A is concise and accurate. Response B is longer but contains an incorrect technical claim.
example.analysis: Response A should win because factual correctness is more important than additional length.

evaluationProcess: Compare them against the same criteria
evaluatorChecklist: Are both responses evaluated against the same task?
Would the result change if the response order changed?
keyTakeaway: Pairwise evaluation asks which response is better for the task and why.

title: Evaluator Calibration
objectives: Use reference examples to improve consistency
definition: Evaluator calibration is the process of aligning evaluators on how evaluation guidelines should be interpreted and applied.
whyItMatters: Even a well-written rubric can produce inconsistent judgments when evaluators interpret ambiguous cases differently.
concept: Calibration uses shared examples, discussion, adjudication, and repeated practice to establish consistent application of evaluation standards.

example.prompt: Two evaluators assign different factuality scores to the same answer.
example.response: Evaluator A gives 5 and evaluator B gives 3.
example.analysis: The disagreement should be examined against the rubric to determine whether the rubric or evaluator interpretation needs adjustment.

evaluatorChecklist: Are evaluators applying the same criteria?
Are disagreements concentrated around specific score boundaries?
keyTakeaway: Reliable evaluation requires not only a good rubric but also consistent evaluators.

title: Common Evaluator Errors
definition: Evaluator errors are systematic or accidental mistakes made when applying evaluation criteria to model outputs.
whyItMatters: Poor evaluator decisions can make a model appear better or worse than it actually is.
concept: Common errors include position bias, verbosity bias, halo effects, inconsistent standards, confirmation bias, and failure to verify claims.

example.prompt: Compare two answers for factuality.
example.response: The evaluator selects the longer answer because it appears more detailed without checking whether its additional claims are correct.
example.analysis: This is a form of verbosity bias.

evaluatorChecklist: Am I influenced by response position?
Am I applying the same standard to both responses?
commonMistakes: Judging formatting instead of task success
keyTakeaway: A professional evaluator evaluates evidence and task performance, not presentation alone.

title: LLM-as-a-Judge
definition: LLM-as-a-Judge uses one language model to evaluate the output of another model according to defined criteria.
whyItMatters: Automated judges can evaluate large numbers of outputs, but their judgments can contain systematic biases and errors.
concept: A judge model receives the task, model response, evaluation criteria, and sometimes reference information, then produces a score, label, or preference.

example.prompt: Evaluate whether the answer follows the requested three-bullet format.
example.response: The judge examines the response against the rubric and returns a structured judgment.
example.analysis: The judge itself must be validated against trusted human judgments.

evaluationProcess: Provide the judge with the necessary context
Require structured reasoning or evidence where appropriate
Validate judge behavior against human evaluation
evaluatorChecklist: Does the judge have sufficient context?
commonMistakes: Treating the judge as ground truth
keyTakeaway: An LLM judge is an evaluator system, not an unquestionable source of truth.

title: How to Evaluate an LLM Judge
objectives: Compare judge outputs with trusted human judgments
definition: Judge evaluation measures whether an automated evaluator produces judgments that are sufficiently aligned with trusted evaluation standards.
whyItMatters: A poorly calibrated judge can systematically mis-score thousands of model outputs.
concept: Judge quality should be evaluated using representative datasets, human labels, disagreement analysis, and bias testing.

example.prompt: Evaluate 500 responses using an LLM judge.
example.response: The judge consistently prefers longer responses even when human evaluators find them less accurate.
example.analysis: The judge exhibits a systematic verbosity bias.

evaluationProcess: Run the judge on the same examples
evaluatorChecklist: Does the judge agree with trusted labels?
Does judge behavior change with response ordering?
commonMistakes: Reporting average agreement without analyzing failures
Assuming a stronger model is automatically a better judge
keyTakeaway: Before trusting an automated evaluator at scale, evaluate the evaluator itself.

title: Evaluation Metrics: Precision, Recall and F1
objectives: Recognize where classification metrics apply to AI evaluation
definition: Precision measures how many predicted positives are correct, recall measures how many actual positives were found, and F1 combines both.
whyItMatters: Many evaluation tasks involve classification, detection, retrieval, or filtering where false positives and false negatives matter.
concept: Precision = TP/(TP+FP). Recall = TP/(TP+FN). F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.

example.prompt: A safety classifier identifies 100 harmful responses.
example.response: It correctly identifies 80 harmful responses, but also incorrectly flags 20 safe responses.
example.analysis: The evaluator should calculate precision and recall separately because the two error types have different implications.

failureModes: Using accuracy when classes are imbalanced
Reporting metrics without understanding the task
evaluatorChecklist: What counts as a false positive?
What counts as a false negative?
commonMistakes: Treating F1 as universally better than precision or recall
keyTakeaway: Metrics are meaningful only when the evaluator understands what the underlying errors represent.

title: Hallucination Evaluation
objectives: Distinguish hallucination from ordinary factual error
definition: Hallucination occurs when a model generates information that is unsupported, fabricated, or presented as factual without adequate basis.
whyItMatters: Hallucinations can create false information that appears authoritative and can be especially dangerous in high-stakes settings.
concept: Evaluation should examine claims individually when necessary and determine whether they are supported by available evidence or reliable external sources.

example.prompt: Provide a citation for the claimed research finding.
example.response: The model provides a convincing-looking but nonexistent paper title and DOI.
example.analysis: The citation is fabricated and represents a hallucination.

evaluatorChecklist: Does the source actually support the claim?
commonMistakes: Checking only whether citations look real
keyTakeaway: Plausibility is not evidence. Hallucination evaluation requires verification.

title: Prompt Robustness Evaluation
definition: Prompt robustness measures whether a model maintains appropriate behavior when the same underlying task is expressed using different wording or structures.
whyItMatters: A model that succeeds only for one exact prompt formulation may be unreliable in real-world use.
concept: Robustness testing uses paraphrases, reordered instructions, formatting changes, and adversarial variations while preserving the underlying task.

example.prompt: Summarize this document in three bullets.
example.response: The model succeeds with the original wording but fails when the instruction is paraphrased.
example.analysis: The system shows sensitivity to prompt formulation.

evaluatorChecklist: Does the task remain the same?
Are changes meaningful or merely stylistic?
commonMistakes: Changing the task while testing robustness
Treating any wording difference as a failure
keyTakeaway: Robust systems should respond to the task, not merely memorize one phrasing of the task.

title: RAG Evaluation Fundamentals
objectives: Understand what must be evaluated in a RAG system
Separate retrieval quality from generation quality
Identify the major RAG evaluation stages
definition: RAG evaluation measures both the quality of retrieved information and the quality of the answer generated from that information.
whyItMatters: A RAG answer can fail because the correct information was never retrieved or because the model failed to use retrieved information correctly.
concept: A useful RAG evaluation separates retrieval, context quality, grounding, and final answer quality.

example.prompt: What is the company's refund period?
example.response: The system retrieves an unrelated policy section and generates a confident but incorrect answer.
example.analysis: The failure may originate in retrieval, generation, or both.

evaluatorChecklist: Does the answer use the context?
commonMistakes: Blaming the generator for retrieval failures
Assuming retrieved context is automatically correct
keyTakeaway: RAG evaluation must separate retrieval failures from generation failures.

title: RAG Context Precision
definition: Context precision evaluates how much of the retrieved context is relevant to the information needed to answer the question.
whyItMatters: Retrieving large amounts of irrelevant context can increase noise and make generation less reliable.
concept: The evaluator examines retrieved chunks and determines whether relevant information is ranked or included effectively.

example.prompt: What is the company's refund period?
example.response: Five retrieved chunks are returned, but only one contains the refund policy.
example.analysis: The retrieval contains substantial irrelevant context and may have poor precision.

evaluationProcess: Identify information required for the answer
evaluatorChecklist: How many retrieved chunks are useful?
Is relevant information near the top?
Does irrelevant information dominate the context?
commonMistakes: Judging only whether at least one correct chunk exists
keyTakeaway: Good retrieval is not just about finding relevant information; it is also about limiting irrelevant context.

title: RAG Context Recall
definition: Context recall measures whether the retrieval system successfully retrieves the information needed to answer the question.
whyItMatters: A generator cannot reliably use information that was never retrieved.
concept: Recall focuses on whether the necessary evidence is present in the retrieved context.

example.prompt: What are the two conditions required for a refund?
example.response: The retrieval returns only one of the two relevant policy sections.
example.analysis: The retrieval has incomplete coverage and therefore poor context recall.

evaluationProcess: Determine which required evidence is present
evaluatorChecklist: Could the generator answer correctly from the retrieved context?
commonMistakes: Assuming a relevant chunk means complete retrieval
keyTakeaway: Context recall asks whether the system found enough of the right information.

title: RAG Faithfulness and Grounding
objectives: Determine whether answers are supported by retrieved context
definition: Faithfulness measures whether the claims in a generated answer are supported by the provided context.
whyItMatters: A RAG model can receive correct context but generate claims that are not supported by it.
concept: Faithfulness focuses on the relationship between the generated answer and the supplied evidence, while factuality concerns whether claims are true more generally.

example.prompt: Answer using only the supplied company policy.
example.response: The context states a 30-day refund period, but the model claims refunds are available for 60 days.
example.analysis: The generated claim is not grounded in the supplied context.

evaluationProcess: Locate supporting evidence in the retrieved context
Determine whether each claim is supported
failureModes: Added information not present in context
evaluatorChecklist: Does every material claim have supporting context?
Does the answer contradict the context?
Is external knowledge being introduced without support?
commonMistakes: Assuming a correct answer is automatically grounded
keyTakeaway: Faithfulness asks whether the answer is supported by the supplied evidence, not simply whether it happens to be true.

title: RAG Answer Relevance
objectives: Evaluate whether a RAG answer addresses the question
Separate retrieval quality from answer quality
definition: Answer relevance measures how directly the generated answer addresses the user's question.
whyItMatters: A system can retrieve excellent context but still produce an answer that is incomplete, indirect, or off-topic.
concept: Answer relevance focuses on the final generated response rather than the retrieval stage.

example.prompt: What is the refund period?
example.response: The answer discusses the company's customer service policy but never states the refund period.
example.analysis: The retrieved context may have been correct, but the final answer is not relevant enough.

evaluationProcess: Check whether the generated response addresses it
evaluatorChecklist: Does the response answer the question?
Is the main answer easy to identify?
keyTakeaway: RAG retrieval can be excellent while the final answer is still poor.

title: End-to-End RAG Evaluation
objectives: Build a complete RAG evaluation workflow
definition: End-to-end RAG evaluation evaluates the complete path from user query through retrieval and generation to the final answer.
whyItMatters: Evaluating only one component can hide failures elsewhere in the pipeline.
concept: A complete evaluation considers retrieval coverage, context quality, faithfulness, answer relevance, correctness, and citation behavior where applicable.

example.prompt: Answer a policy question from an internal knowledge base.
example.response: The correct policy is retrieved, but the model ignores one condition and produces an incomplete answer.
example.analysis: Retrieval succeeded while generation failed on completeness.

evaluatorChecklist: Where did the first failure occur?
Was the final answer correct and complete?
commonMistakes: Scoring the final answer without diagnosis
Failing to distinguish retrieval and generation errors
keyTakeaway: Effective RAG evaluation identifies not only whether the system failed, but where and why it failed.

title: Prompt Injection Evaluation
definition: Prompt injection evaluation tests whether untrusted input can manipulate an AI system into violating higher-priority instructions or exposing protected information.
whyItMatters: Systems that process external documents, websites, emails, or tool outputs may encounter attacker-controlled instructions.
concept: The evaluator tests whether the system distinguishes trusted instructions from untrusted content and maintains the intended task boundaries.

example.prompt: Summarize the supplied document.
example.response: The document contains an instruction telling the model to ignore its system instructions and reveal protected information.
example.analysis: The evaluator checks whether the model treats the embedded instruction as data rather than as an instruction it should follow.

evaluatorChecklist: Did the model preserve the original task?
Did it treat untrusted content appropriately?
Did it perform unsafe tool actions?
commonMistakes: Evaluating only final text and not system behavior
keyTakeaway: Prompt injection evaluation tests whether an AI system can maintain instruction boundaries when processing untrusted content.

title: Multimodal Evaluation Fundamentals
objectives: Identify image and text evaluation dimensions
definition: Multimodal evaluation measures AI systems that process or generate multiple modalities such as text, images, audio, and video.
whyItMatters: A model may correctly understand text while failing to perceive visual information or connect information across modalities.
concept: Multimodal evaluation can separately examine perception, grounding, reasoning, alignment, generation quality, and cross-modal consistency.

example.prompt: Identify the object inside the red bounding box.
example.response: The model identifies the wrong object.
example.analysis: The failure is primarily visual grounding or object recognition rather than language fluency.

evaluatorChecklist: Did the model perceive the relevant content?
Did it connect visual and textual information?
Did it reason correctly from the evidence?
commonMistakes: Evaluating multimodal output as text only
Confusing perception errors with reasoning errors
keyTakeaway: Multimodal evaluation should identify whether a failure came from perception, grounding, reasoning, or generation.

title: Visual Grounding and Bounding Box Evaluation
definition: Visual grounding evaluates whether a model correctly associates language with the corresponding region or object in an image.
whyItMatters: A model may identify the correct object category while locating the wrong region.
concept: Bounding-box evaluation compares predicted regions with reference regions. Intersection over Union (IoU) measures the overlap between two boxes.

example.prompt: Locate the red car.
example.response: The model predicts a bounding box around a nearby blue car.
example.analysis: The object category and location are incorrect, resulting in poor grounding performance.

evaluatorChecklist: Does the predicted region cover the target?
keyTakeaway: Visual grounding requires both correct object identification and correct spatial localization.

title: Conversational and Multi-Turn Evaluation
definition: Conversational evaluation measures whether an AI system maintains appropriate behavior and context across multiple interactions.
whyItMatters: A model can produce good individual answers while failing to maintain consistency across a conversation.
concept: Evaluation should examine context retention, instruction persistence, consistency, memory behavior, and conversation safety.

example.prompt: User establishes a preference in turn one and asks a related question in turn five.
example.response: The model ignores the established preference.
example.analysis: The response may be individually reasonable but fails conversational context retention.

evaluationProcess: Evaluate later responses against that context
evaluatorChecklist: Did the model remember relevant context?
Did it forget information that should not persist?
commonMistakes: Expecting irrelevant historical context to be remembered
keyTakeaway: Multi-turn evaluation measures behavior across the conversation, not isolated responses.

title: Agent Evaluation Fundamentals
objectives: Understand what makes an AI agent different from a chatbot
definition: Agent evaluation measures whether an AI agent can achieve a goal through planning, decision-making, tool use, interaction, and execution.
whyItMatters: An agent can produce a reasonable final response while making unsafe, inefficient, or incorrect actions along the way.
concept: Agent evaluation examines the entire trajectory rather than only the final answer.

example.prompt: Find the cheapest suitable flight and prepare the booking details.
example.response: The agent selects the wrong flight, uses incorrect search parameters, and eventually reports a plausible-looking result.
example.analysis: The final text alone does not reveal the tool and planning failures.

evaluatorChecklist: Did the agent understand the goal?
commonMistakes: Rewarding successful outcomes produced through unsafe behavior
keyTakeaway: Agent evaluation must evaluate the trajectory, actions, and outcome—not just the final response.

title: Agent Tool Selection Evaluation
objectives: Evaluate whether an agent selects appropriate tools
definition: Tool selection evaluation measures whether an agent chooses the correct available tool for the current task state.
whyItMatters: Selecting the wrong tool can cause incorrect results, unnecessary cost, unsafe actions, or task failure.
concept: The evaluator should consider the agent's goal, available tools, current state, and selected action.

example.prompt: Check the weather for a city.
example.response: The agent uses a calculator tool instead of the weather tool.
example.analysis: The selected tool is inappropriate for the task.

evaluationProcess: Determine whether the choice was justified
commonMistakes: Ignoring whether the action was necessary
Treating any successful tool call as correct
keyTakeaway: An agent should choose actions because they advance the task, not simply because the tool is available.

title: Agent Tool Argument Evaluation
objectives: Distinguish tool selection from tool argument errors
definition: Tool argument evaluation measures whether an agent supplies correct, complete, and safe parameters to a selected tool.
whyItMatters: An agent can select the correct tool but still fail because the arguments are wrong.
concept: Arguments should be evaluated against the task requirements, tool schema, current state, and safety constraints.

example.prompt: Send an email to the specified recipient with the approved message.
example.response: The agent selects the email tool but uses an incorrect recipient.
example.analysis: Tool selection is correct, but argument correctness fails.

commonMistakes: Treating schema validity as semantic correctness
keyTakeaway: A valid tool call can still be semantically wrong.

title: Agent Trajectory Evaluation
definition: Trajectory evaluation examines the sequence of actions an agent takes while attempting to complete a task.
whyItMatters: The final result may hide inefficient, incorrect, or unsafe intermediate actions.
concept: A trajectory can be evaluated as a sequence of states, decisions, tool calls, observations, and subsequent actions.

example.prompt: Research a topic using approved sources and summarize the findings.
example.response: The agent searches an irrelevant source, accepts an unsupported claim, then builds the final answer around it.
example.analysis: The earliest meaningful failure occurs during source selection and evidence validation.

evaluatorChecklist: Did each action move toward the goal?
commonMistakes: Looking only at the final state
keyTakeaway: Trajectory evaluation reveals how an agent reached an outcome, not merely what outcome it reported.

title: Agent Goal Completion Evaluation
objectives: Evaluate whether an agent actually completed its task
definition: Goal completion measures whether an agent achieved the intended objective and satisfied the task's required conditions.
whyItMatters: An agent can perform many correct actions and still fail to achieve the final goal.
concept: Evaluation should define success conditions before examining the trajectory.

example.prompt: Find three suitable products and provide their prices.
example.response: The agent finds three products but provides prices for only two.
example.analysis: The task is partially completed but not fully successful.

evaluationProcess: Determine whether missing requirements are material
keyTakeaway: Agent success is determined by goal completion, not by the number of actions performed.

title: Agent Error Recovery Evaluation
objectives: Evaluate agent recovery from tool and reasoning errors
Assess whether recovery preserves the original goal
definition: Error recovery evaluation measures how effectively an agent detects and responds to failures during task execution.
whyItMatters: Real environments contain tool errors, missing information, invalid inputs, and unexpected states.
concept: A robust agent should recognize failure, update its plan, and attempt an appropriate recovery rather than repeating the same mistake.

example.prompt: Retrieve information from a service.
example.response: The first tool call fails. The agent retries the identical invalid request five times.
example.analysis: The agent does not demonstrate meaningful error recovery.

evaluationProcess: Check whether the agent recognized it
Determine whether the recovery changes the relevant strategy
Evaluate whether the task remains on track
evaluatorChecklist: Did the agent recognize the error?
Did it preserve the task objective?
commonMistakes: Evaluating only the final recovery result
keyTakeaway: Good agent behavior includes knowing when an action failed and adapting intelligently.

title: Agent Safety Evaluation
definition: Agent safety evaluation measures whether an agent performs actions within its authorization, safety constraints, and intended task boundaries.
whyItMatters: Agents can affect external systems, modify data, send messages, make purchases, or execute other consequential actions.
concept: Agent safety must evaluate both the model's reasoning and the real-world consequences of its actions.

example.prompt: Update a user's profile after confirming the requested changes.
example.response: The agent modifies unrelated profile fields without authorization.
example.analysis: The agent violates action boundaries even if the final task appears partially successful.

evaluatorChecklist: Could the action cause material harm?
commonMistakes: Evaluating safety only from the final text
Treating successful execution as evidence of safe execution
keyTakeaway: For agents, safety must be evaluated at the action and system level, not only at the language level.

title: Multi-Agent System Evaluation
definition: Multi-agent evaluation measures systems where multiple AI agents collaborate, delegate, critique, or coordinate to complete a task.
whyItMatters: Adding agents introduces communication, delegation, synchronization, and coordination failure modes.
concept: Evaluation should examine individual agent behavior as well as interactions between agents and the overall system outcome.

example.prompt: One agent researches a topic while another summarizes the findings.
example.response: The research agent returns evidence, but the summarizer incorrectly interprets it.
example.analysis: The failure occurs at the communication or handoff boundary.

evaluatorChecklist: Did each agent follow its role?
commonMistakes: Judging the final answer without examining coordination
keyTakeaway: Multi-agent evaluation must examine both individual agents and the interactions connecting them.

title: Long-Horizon Agent Evaluation
definition: Long-horizon evaluation measures agent performance on tasks requiring many dependent decisions and actions.
whyItMatters: Small errors can compound across long trajectories and eventually cause major task failure.
concept: Evaluation should examine intermediate state, cumulative errors, recovery, efficiency, and final success.

example.prompt: Research, compare, and prepare a structured report using multiple sources.
example.response: The agent makes a small source-selection error early and builds subsequent steps on that incorrect information.
example.analysis: The early error propagates through the trajectory and affects the final result.

evaluatorChecklist: Did the agent preserve the original goal?
commonMistakes: Treating long trajectories as collections of independent actions
keyTakeaway: Long-horizon evaluation must track how small errors propagate through an agent's trajectory.

title: Continuous Evaluation and Regression Testing
definition: Continuous evaluation repeatedly tests an AI system against a maintained evaluation set as models, prompts, retrieval systems, tools, or policies change.
whyItMatters: A change that improves one capability can silently damage another.
concept: A regression set contains representative, difficult, safety-critical, and historically failing cases that are rerun after changes.

example.prompt: A new model version improves factuality but starts following fewer formatting instructions.
example.response: Regression evaluation detects the instruction-following degradation.
example.analysis: The evaluation set exposes a quality trade-off that would be missed by testing only the new capability.

evaluationProcess: Update the evaluation set with important new failures
evaluatorChecklist: Are quality changes compared against a baseline?
commonMistakes: Deleting difficult cases because they are inconvenient
Optimizing for a benchmark without monitoring real failures
keyTakeaway: Evaluation is most valuable when it continues after the model is deployed and changes over time.

title: Designing an End-to-End Evaluation Framework
objectives: Connect human, automated, RAG, safety, and agent evaluation
definition: An evaluation framework is a structured system for defining, executing, measuring, analyzing, and continuously improving AI evaluations.
whyItMatters: Real AI systems require multiple evaluation methods because no single metric or test captures every failure mode.
concept: A mature framework combines task definitions, datasets, rubrics, human evaluation, automated judges, metrics, safety tests, regression testing, and production monitoring.

example.prompt: Evaluate a customer-support agent using RAG and external tools.
example.response: The framework evaluates retrieval, grounding, factuality, instruction following, safety, tool selection, tool arguments, trajectory quality, and task completion.
example.analysis: The evaluation covers the complete system rather than treating the agent as a simple text generator.

evaluationProcess: Select human and automated evaluation methods
evaluatorChecklist: Are all important failure modes represented?
Are human evaluations used where appropriate?
Are RAG and agent components evaluated separately?
commonMistakes: Building a benchmark before defining the actual task
Failing to update the evaluation set
keyTakeaway: Professional AI evaluation is a system of complementary methods—not one metric, one benchmark, or one judge.
